entities.name: San Leonardo da Porto Maurizio
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
San Leonardo da Porto Maurizio (1676-1751) is an Italian Franciscan friar, missionary, and Catholic saint who was one of the most prolific 18th-century promoters of the Stations of the Cross (Via Crucis) — establishing over 570 Stations of the Cross throughout the Italian peninsula during his missionary career, including the celebrated Stations of the Cross in the Colosseum (Rome), where he preached to enormous crowds — and who became one of the most popular preachers and missionaries of 18th-century Italy, canonized in 1867 and proclaimed patron of popular missionaries by Pope Pius XII.

Leonardo da Porto Maurizio's missionary work in Italy (1709-1751) was extraordinary in its scale and impact: he traveled throughout Tuscany, Liguria, Umbria, Genoa, and Corsica conducting missions — popular preaching campaigns that could draw crowds of thousands for days — focused on repentance, confession, and devotion to the Eucharist and the Passion of Christ. His promotion of the Stations of the Cross was his most distinctive contribution; he viewed the Via Crucis as the perfect devotional practice for lay Catholics, accessible and portable in a way that longer liturgical forms were not.

The Colosseum Stations of the Cross, which Leonardo established in 1749, remained in use until the 20th century and are among the most famous devotional uses of an ancient Roman monument. His canonization in 1867 during the tumultuous period of Italian unification gave his legacy additional significance, as his popular Franciscan missions represented a model of Catholic spiritual vitality in contrast to the political upheaval of the Risorgimento.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: San Leonardo da Porto Maurizio — the most prolific promoter of the Stations of the Cross in history (570+ installations), preacher at the Colosseum, and canonized model of popular Catholic missions — is historically significant for transforming the Via Crucis into the most widespread lay devotional practice in 18th-century Italy.
